title: Prize-winning image which sparked backlash was AI-generated, Nikon rules
key_facts: Nikon disqualified the winner of its Small World In Motion contest, which accepts microscope photos and video, after scientists said the winning video looked fake.
Nikon said the use of generative AI in the composition of the video broke the contest rules, and that this was not a judgement of the entrant's reputation or scientific contributions.
The winner was Dr Ning Xu of Tsinghua University, with a video of hair-like cilia moving in the airway of a child with the lung condition PCD.
Xu had acknowledged using AI but said he believed he acted within the rules and cooperated with the investigation.
Dr Robert Hirst of the University of Leicester, lead scientist for the NHS PCD diagnosis centre, said the cells and cilia 'look nothing like those from PCD patients'.
Nikon will now review the rules and procedures of the contest, which has run for 15 years.
quote_evidence: The firm said the video "did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI", but added it was not a judgement of the entrant's professional reputation or scientific contributions.
Xu had acknowledged using AI, but said he believed he had acted within the rules, and had cooperated with Nikon's investigation.
Hirst, who is lead scientist for the NHS centre for PCD diagnosis at the university, said the cells and cilia "look nothing like those from PCD patients".
why_it_matters_hint: A scientific image contest shows the rules and checks around AI-made media are being tested in public.
event_date: 9 Oct 2026 (BBC publication date; date of the ruling not stated)
notes: Nikon's statement is quoted by BBC. Headline says 'AI-generated'; the text says generative AI was used in composing the video, and Xu says he thought he was within the rules.
